Maladaptive Strategies.value: never allow myself to feel or express anger
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
issues.explanation: For trauma involving a child's life-threatening illness, revenge-focused ideation about identifiable responsible people is hard to reconcile unless there was clear culpability (e.g. negligence), which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It appears clinically mismatched to the stated trauma context.

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: Generalized threat from strangers and scanning faces for danger fit interpersonal assault or public violence better than a child's medical crisis. These threat items imply fear of hostile people in ordinary situations, but the rest of the profile does not provide a coherent bridge from the illness trauma to stranger-based danger expectations.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: Intense rage on recall could occur, but here it primarily supports the revenge item and interpersonal-threat theme. In combination with the stranger-threat items, it pulls the profile toward an assault/perpetrator formulation rather than a child's illness trauma formulation.

issues.item: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me
issues.explanation: Meaning seeking is not inherently maladaptive and, in this profile, sits awkwardly with the otherwise threat-trigger-memory driven formulation; it does not clearly function as an avoidance/safety strategy tied to the selected triggers, threat items, or memory pattern.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance for interpersonal threat in faces/body language is difficult to reconcile with the trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, where danger is more plausibly linked to medical cues, loss cues, or signs of illness rather than hostile people.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: Needing to stay alert to fall asleep implies ongoing external danger monitoring; for a trauma centered on a child's illness, this would usually require clearer linkage to caregiving/medical monitoring, which is absent from the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: For the indexed trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, 'anything that reminds me of someone I have lost' implies bereavement/loss rather than ongoing threat or illness trauma. That is a hard-to-explain mismatch unless the child died, which is not the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: Within the overall profile, the dominant theme is fear/hypervigilance/disorientation around threat cues (sirens, crying, startle, sleep vigilance, physical reactivity, confused/unreal memory). 'Intense rage' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the rest of the profile and sits awkwardly beside suppression of anger, making this item clinically less coherent than the others.

vignette:
Omar was twenty-five years old, a data scientist who spent his days in a quiet, open-plan office, building predictive models. It was a job he had chosen precisely because it felt safe: predictable, controlled, full of patterns he could see coming. But safety, he had learned, was an illusion. Three years ago, his younger sister, then twelve, had been rushed to the emergency room with a septic infection that had gone undiagnosed for nearly two days. He had been the one to find her in the morning, her skin hot and damp, her breathing shallow, her eyes wild with a fever that had already begun to shut down her kidneys. He had called the ambulance, and he had ridden with her, holding her hand as the sirens screamed through the predawn streets.

The memory of that ride was not a single, coherent film in his mind. It came to him in fragments that he could never quite arrange in the right order. He remembered the paramedic's voice, then the smell of sweat and antiseptic, then the way his sister's fingers had gone limp, then the siren again, but he could not tell which came first or what connected them. The whole thing felt, when he tried to hold it in his mind, like something that had happened to someone else-so extreme, so violent in its suddenness, that it was hard to believe it had actually happened to him. But then a sound would yank him back into it. A car horn. A sudden clatter in the office kitchen. And he would be right there again, in the back of the ambulance, heart pounding, breath gone, the same raw terror flooding his chest as if no time had passed at all.

He had built his life around not going back there. He never allowed himself to feel anger-not even the quiet, justified irritation that came with office politics or bad drivers. Anger felt like a door he could not open without letting everything else out. He also tried very hard not to think about the trauma. When a memory surfaced, he would immediately redirect his attention to a spreadsheet, a podcast, a Sudoku puzzle-anything to keep the story from playing out. But the most visible cost was his avoidance of anything medical. He had not set foot in a hospital since that week. He had cancelled three routine physicals. He changed his route to work to avoid the street where the ambulance had picked them up. When a colleague mentioned a doctor's appointment, Omar felt his stomach drop and his palms go slick with sweat.

The physical reactions were the hardest to hide. At night, he could not fall asleep without feeling like he had to stay alert, as if something terrible would happen the moment he let his guard down. He slept in short, shallow bursts, waking at the slightest noise. During the day, ordinary sounds that would not bother most people-a chair scraping, a door slamming, someone clearing their throat too loudly-would make him jump as if a gun had gone off. He had come to believe that his body had been permanently rewired, that he was now a person who could not trust the world to stay quiet.

What finally brought him to seek help was not the startle response or the sleeplessness, but a moment at work. A junior analyst had started crying in the breakroom after a difficult meeting. The sound of her crying-that wet, ragged intake of breath-had sent Omar into a full-blown panic attack. He had locked himself in the bathroom, shaking, his sister's face superimposed over the present moment, the terror as fresh as if it were happening again. His manager found him and told him, kindly, that he needed to take care of himself. So here he was, sitting in a therapist's office, terrified that if he started to talk about it, he would fall apart completely. But he was also, quietly, desperately hoping that maybe, for the first time in three years, he could learn to sleep through the night without listening for sirens.
